newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to revamp budget because of cash troubles.
newsitem.headline: Russia to revamp budget because of cash troubles.

text.p: The Russian government, acknowledging it cannot afford to fund the 1997 budget signed less than two months ago, agreed Friday on a broad plan of spending cuts, a spokeswoman said.

The proposed cuts, which have to be approved by parliament, could lead to a new battle between the executive and the communist-dominated legislature, where many deputies have vowed to resist cutbacks in social spending.
The government's move followed a series of official announcements in recent days that Moscow has fallen far short of its revenue targets for the first three months of 1997.
On Friday it also discussed a new tax code, to go into force in 1998 at the earliest, which it hopes will both simplify the current complex system and boost future revenues.
Details of the budget cuts were not released Friday. A spokeswoman said only that the government had agreed in principle to a Finance Ministry proposal to cut 1997 spending.

Last week, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said that government revenues in the first quarter were only 57 percent of budgeted levels. The original 1997 budget calls for revenue of 434 trillion roubles ($77 billion).

As a result, Russia has been unable to meet many of its funding obligations, forcing delays in paying salaries to a wide range of workers from teachers to tax inspectors, and leaving many programmes badly underfunded.

Among the embarrassing shortfalls has been Moscow's inability to fund the Alpha international space station. Some American legislators say delays on a Russian module where cosmonauts will live could jeopardise the entire programme.

The budget cuts and moves to reshape the country's tax system could pave the way to receiving fresh foreign cash and help the newly reshuffled government proceed with radical market reforms which President Boris Yeltsin has vowed to support.
The International Monetary Fund has said it will not give any more funds from its $10 billion three-year loan until the cabinet agrees on the tax code.
